98897be0-18bb-5f36-beaa-b28285fbeb42.name: Earring.
98897be0-18bb-5f36-beaa-b28285fbeb42.description:
The main pendant-ring has an opening for insertion in the earlobe. Attached at the lower edge of this ring and pointing downwards are three spheres, each joined to the other and each extended at the base into cylindrical projections. These forms are decorated with radial grooves and lateral bands. Pointing upwards from the same lower part of the ring is a short spoke coiled at the top. Its purpose is unknown.  
These spherical shapes may well occur in some Muslim jewellery from both Eastern and Western areas, but we have not found anything similar to the Raqqada earring in the various collections that we have seen. Only a very few pieces of jewellery from the early centuries of Islam survive. Tombs have not yielded much and Islamic religious institutions do not have treasures like Christian churches do.  
The dearth of documentation makes affiliation, evolutionary research and the dating of new finds within a coherent series very difficult. Things become clearer from the AH 5th / AD 11th century.
98897be0-18bb-5f36-beaa-b28285fbeb42.short_description: Although their spherical shape is similar to other Eastern and Western Islamic jewellery, these earrings are different from Raqqada Zirid and Fatimid pieces in their technique and decoration. Only a small quantity of jewellery has survived from the early centuries of Islam to enable them to be dated.
98897be0-18bb-5f36-beaa-b28285fbeb42.method_for_datation: This earring was found during the excavations undertaken in the 1960s on the Raqqada site. Raqqada was founded by the Aghlabids in the year 263 / 876. Its active life as a city continued up to the mid-5th / 11th century, when it was sacked by the Hilalian tribes. So the date of the earring could fall anywhere over the span of these two centuries. We unfortunately do not possess any information as to which archaeological layer the piece came from. However, this piece is technically and decoratively different from Fatimid and Zirid pendants. It has a more archaic and a definitely more classical appearance, which leads us to date it to between the 3rd and the early 4th centuries (9th to 10th centuries).
98897be0-18bb-5f36-beaa-b28285fbeb42.obtention: The earring was discovered on the Raqqada site, this earring was kept at the Institut National du Patrimoine de Kairouan. It was acquired by the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada in 1993 and displayed there.
98897be0-18bb-5f36-beaa-b28285fbeb42.bibliography: *Ifriqiya: Thirteen Centuries of Art and Architecture in Tunisia*, pp.174–6.
98897be0-18bb-5f36-beaa-b28285fbeb42.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Adornment; geometric decoration; jewellery

98b84854-315a-5209-aff7-d359b94d60f4.name: Amulet
98b84854-315a-5209-aff7-d359b94d60f4.short_description: This gold amulet case is inscribed on both sides with verses from the Qur’an in an early *kufic* script. The magical-religious properties of amulets are accepted in the Islamic world and are reinforced by the use of verses from the Qur’an. In this case verses are from chapter CXII entitled ‘Sincerity’ extolling God’s purity and devotion to the one God.
keywords: Amulet; Kufic; Quran; Gold; talisman

9973d81a-f2f0-5d4a-892f-127dedae62bc.name: Hujul (Bracelet) with Chased Decoration
9973d81a-f2f0-5d4a-892f-127dedae62bc.short_description: This *Hujul* (Bracelet) from the Al-Busaid Dynasty showcases one of Oman's oldest design elements, circles with central dots, with early use on shell jewellery dated to the 4th millennium BC. More complex dot-in-circle patterns are found on 3rd and 2nd millennium BC soft-stone vessels where they are typically arranged in rows and combined with linear elements. Today, dot-in-circle patterns continue to be used by Omani artisans and are seen on wooden drums, axe blades and knife scabbards of the Musandam Peninsula, on the silver jewellery of northern Oman and on the pottery of Dhofar.
9973d81a-f2f0-5d4a-892f-127dedae62bc.obtention: Museum of the Ministry of Heritage and Culture

9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.name: Bridal breast jewellery (*Chaprag*)
9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.short_description: This exquisite article called a *chaprag* shows the exceptional skill and inventiveness of the unknown goldsmith, who makes each piece of jewellery a virtual work of art in itself. The *chaprag* is a breast ornament consisting of a round plate and tiny chains. It is executed in filigree technique and adorned with decorative stones. Besides its decorative function, it was applied for the purpose of fastening the cleavage of the tunic. It was characteristic of the Ohrid-Prespa region, that is, the areas of Ohridsko Pole, Strushko Pole and Debarski Drimkol.
9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.author: Milena Petrovic, ethnologist

9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.name: Belt
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.short_description: A Circassian belt with 15 silver and niello-decorated buckles connected together to form the belt; there is a rosette shape at the end with locking mechanism and three dangling silver tassels. This belt, together with the dagger, was an accessory forming the traditional male Circassian dress. The Circassians used to carry daggers which were an essential part of the national dress. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries with which they had spiritual and religious links.
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities

9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.name: Pendant.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.description: A gold crescent-shaped pendant with enamel work. Two bands of delicate gold filigree work surround a panel of cloisonné enamel with a symmetrical design of two birds arranged on either side of a tree. The pendant may have been hung with strings of pearls from the three loops along the bottom. The enamel inset imitates Byzantine designs. Gold jewellery from Byzantium was known in Fatimid Egypt originating either from Byzantine craftsmen who immigrated to Egypt or through diplomatic gifts sent by Byzantine rulers. In 1046 the Fatimid Caliph al-Mustansir (r.1036–94) received a large gift from the Emperor of Byzantium which included hundreds of gold vessels, brocade and gold-embroidered turbans. This exchange of diplomatic gifts is recorded in The Book of Treasures and Gifts, by Ibn Zubayr, written just before the destruction and dispersal of the Fatimid treasury in 1062.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.short_description: Gold jewellery with delicate filigree work was popular during the Fatimid period. Some pieces, such as this pendant, also feature enamel work derived from Byzantine designs. The Fatimid treasury is known to have accumulated a vast hoard of gold objects that included jewellery.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.method_for_datation: The pendant resembles other gold jewellery from the Fatimid era; generally small in size and often decorated with filigree work, cloisonné enamel, or niello. From the mid-11th century figurative elements began to appear, such as birds. The dating of Fatimid jewellery has been derived from excavations in a number of sites, including that at Fustat in Cairo.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.method_for_provenance: The Fatimids were renowned for their rich splendid jewellery. Most of the workmanship would have taken place in Egypt, the political centre of the Fatimid dynasty.

9d4974ab-f811-5127-ae3d-e1895f9c8e80.name: *Hirz* (Necklace) with Qur’an Case
9d4974ab-f811-5127-ae3d-e1895f9c8e80.short_description: A fascination with the possibilities of design within a rectangular format is evident in the myriad interpretations of the *hirz* (necklace) Qur’an case. Squares, rectangles, diamonds and incremental components of triangles are all in widespread use as elements of Omani design. Simple patterns formed by straight, intersecting lines are most easily executed and therefore predominate on the hardest materials – stone, bone, metals and hardwood. In woodwork, angular designs are often faceted, a technique which enhances visual interest through the interplay of light and shadow.

9ee4a0fa-3ad1-5d46-a700-262cfde9d93d.name: Scarab brooch
9ee4a0fa-3ad1-5d46-a700-262cfde9d93d.short_description: Illustrates the influence of Egyptian motifs on Victorian jewellery. Part of the second wave of Egyptianisation, related to the construction of the Suez Canal.

9f21301c-034b-5651-9b4a-fedc9f27510f.name: Ring
9f21301c-034b-5651-9b4a-fedc9f27510f.short_description: This gold ring is embellished with openwork filigree and granulation. On the rectangular bezel, two human figures in frontal position frame a representation of what may be either the tree of life or a fire altar. On the sides are portrayed confronted birds and a crowned male head, the latter reminiscent of similar stylised representations on Persian ceramic ware of the Seljuq period. An identical ring is preserved in the Mayer Institute of Islamic Art in Jerusalem.

9fbdeae7-8d2e-57e7-91e7-ef25446597b8.name: Necklace
9fbdeae7-8d2e-57e7-91e7-ef25446597b8.short_description: Fishing Communities at Ra's al-Hamra (6000—4000 BC) Archaeologists have identified 14 prehistoric sites in the Ra's al-Hamra area of modern - day Muscat dating from 6,000 to 4,000 BC. The sites, commonly known as shell middens, consist of layered deposits resulting from food preparation and consumption of local species including shells, fish remains and the bones of marine and land mammals. The communities of fisher-gatherers that settled in the Ra's al-Hamra area at this time exploited ecological niches related to the sea and the mangrove stands, and also had access to resources of the interior through Wadi Aday. The material culture of these early communities is represented by finds of tools and ornaments made of shells (pendants, beads and fishhooks), mammal bones (beads, points and gorge hooks) and stones (beads, earrings and lithic industry). This object is another example illustrating the dot-in-circle design.
9fbdeae7-8d2e-57e7-91e7-ef25446597b8.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
keywords: Necklace; Jewellery

a104ff6a-9766-59a7-acc1-0e2d2676a230.name: Buckle
a104ff6a-9766-59a7-acc1-0e2d2676a230.description: Silver buckle, chiselled with floral and vegetal motifs, and the application, in golden brass, of an eagle and two hands. This kind of motif as a symbolic protection against the evil eye is reminiscent of the beliefs held before the arrival of the Islamic religion. The eagle is considered to be a symbol of power and the open hand is the most powerful protective existing symbol, but equally it symbolises the five fundamental principles of the Islam. In the North of Africa, the jewels that represented the social status of their carriers have turned into accessible adornment to all the social classes, used with protective character, especially against the evil eye. They are also a symbol of the wealth of a woman when she marries.
keywords: Silver; Jewellery; Protection

a2f21fcb-9dfe-5243-bac8-dcdfef65c883.name: Fly Whisk (*chauri*) with Design of Floral and Vegetal Motifs on the Handle
a2f21fcb-9dfe-5243-bac8-dcdfef65c883.short_description:
A fly whisk with the top of the carved ivory handle in the form of an inverted bell-shaped socket that has two rows of individually carved leaves at its top. The bottom portion of the socket and the top of the handle, which it connects to, are decorated with bands of cypress, iris, and poppy motives. The remaining part of the handle has a long spiral rope pattern and terminates in a knop. The whisk itself is composed of thin flat strips of whale baleen. The handle is made of three separate pieces that disassemble by unscrewing the socket and knop from the center shaft in a clockwise direction.  
There is gray dirt in carved recesses of the handle and around the base of the whisk. There are a number of broken/missing whisk elements.

a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.name: Part of a veil
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.short_description: Five lines of gold ¼ Ottoman lira and other type of coins sewn together on a piece of cloth; such pieces were usually affixed above the nose on the veils, *burqu'*, of women of Beer Sheba. Fashion, local costumes and rites in the territories of Jordan and Palestine show identical elements, as this veil illustrates. It is one of the many examples of jewellery made with Ottoman coins to decorate veils and dresses. Jewellery was an important accessory for married women because pieces of jewellery constituted part of the dowry their husbands gave them for marriage. Jewellery was also a symbol of financial prestige: the more precious it was, the richer the husband’s family. Silver jewellery was the most common because only rich people could afford gold jewellery.
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.author: Huda Kilani

a5b2538f-6e41-5940-b65c-59d0b57a7466.name: Necklace (*lebba*).
a5b2538f-6e41-5940-b65c-59d0b57a7466.description: This large necklace consists of several pendants alternating with fluted ovoid gold pearls on a silk cord. The pendants consist of different golden drops in the shape of fleurons or roses of Rhodes known as *gharnati*, rosettes, crescent moons and stars that come together to form a long broad necklace covering almost the entire chest. The pendants are decorated on both sides, each studded with ten emeralds and garnets on one side and decorated on the other with green, red and blue champlevé enamel with floral and plant decoration. This type of jewellery was worn by brides from Fez on their wedding day and by upper-middle-class women during festivities. The magic symbols that they bear are intended to protect the women against the evil eye. The fact that there are ten precious stones (twice five, the symbol of the hand that protects from harm) and the crescent-and-moon motif, imitating an eyebrow and an iris (the eye that sees danger) indicate the importance that women placed on amulets.
a5b2538f-6e41-5940-b65c-59d0b57a7466.short_description: This necklace, consisting of several pendants decorated on both sides, would have been worn by a bride. It includes symbols intended to protect her against bad luck: the two hands represented by the ten precious stones set in medallions, and the eye represented by the crescent and the circle.

a5b9fc7a-39f3-548a-ab66-613df1cdc6e7.short_description: This pendant was used on the horses of Ottoman officials and indicated their high status and wealth. It is made of a single, lozenge-shaped silver plaque decorated with red coral and blue gemstones. a5f4cf65-f406-56b6-91f6-a6bdbe9b499f.name: Thumb ring
a5f4cf65-f406-56b6-91f6-a6bdbe9b499f.short_description: Archers wore thumb rings made of semi-precious stone on the thumb of their right hand to help them draw their bows. A seminal part of a weapon held in high esteem in the Orient, these richly-embellished thumb rings were ideal expressions of a warrior’s status and wealth.

a65ae972-d872-5b79-975c-3a0ac79cc20b.name: *Shawkah* (Brooche)
a65ae972-d872-5b79-975c-3a0ac79cc20b.short_description: This *Shawkah* (Brooche) is a fine example of squares, rectangles and diamonds and their integral components as a prominent design motif in Omani jewellery. Simple patterns formed by straight, intersecting lines are most easily executed and therefore predominate on the hardest materials – stone, bone, metals and hardwood. In woodwork, angular designs are often faceted, a technique which enhances visual interest through the interplay of light and shadow. Angular patterns are also prevalent in weaving and basketry, where methods of construction dictate the use of linear elements.

a6e39000-fe68-56fd-a598-f2bd48c41311.name: Silver brooch pin
a6e39000-fe68-56fd-a598-f2bd48c41311.description: The small collection of Berber jewellery that Sorolla´s family acquired during their visit to Morocco in February of 1919 includes this silver pin. The pins are indispensable parts of female jewellery; headbands, necklaces, bracelets and earrings complete the outfit. This pin served to fasten clothes to the shoulders and pins were always carried in pairs, connected by a string, which in this case was not preserved. The Museum preserves the other twin.
a6e39000-fe68-56fd-a598-f2bd48c41311.author: Covadonga Pitarch
keywords: North Africa; Silver; Costume; Souvenir

a7d32c3d-fe87-5afb-b350-091e02c5d6d1.name: Pendant
a7d32c3d-fe87-5afb-b350-091e02c5d6d1.short_description: This ivory tooth-shaped amulet, decorated with a series of diagonal parallel lines, comes from the excavations conducted between 1900 to 1901 by David Randall-MacIver and Luigi Pigorini. As a result of earlier excavations by W. Petrie and J. De Morgan, who documented the existence of an era preceding the 1st dynasty, Pigorini, an archaeologist and the director of the "Museo Preistorico Etnografico e Kircheriano", decided to increase the museum’s Egyptian archaeological collection. In 1878 he began to acquire important groups, but the main body of the collection was donated by Randall-MacIver in 1901, from excavations he carried out on the behalf of the Egypt Exploration Fund in the town of el-Amrah, Upper Egypt. Another major purchase — from the Italian Archaeological Mission in Egypt (excavations of Hammamiye) led by Ernesto Schiaparelli, director of the Egyptian Museum in Turin — followed in 1905.  The last main acquisition took place in 1913 when the Egyptian objects from Enrico Hillyer Giglioli’s collection entered the museum collection.

a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.name: Pendant.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.description:
Archaeological excavations in the Egyptian City of Fustat have furnished us with some pieces of jewellery such as bracelets, rings, earrings and pendants of gold and silver. A number of techniques in jewellery-making and ornamentation were widespread in Egypt during the Fatimid period. Some of the most important techniques were carving, piercing and enamel inlay. The piece illustrated here is a good example of decorative enamel inlay.  
Generally, decorative enamelling was done in one of two ways: one way – called lobed enamel – involves pouring the enamel into small metallic lobes, closely resembling moulds. After firing the lobes in a kiln, they are then mounted in specific places in accordance with the design on to the gold surface of the piece of jewellery. The other way involves making deep-grooved decorative carvings of the desired design on the surface of the piece; enamel is then poured into the grooves and the piece is then fired in a kiln. The former method is a quicker and faster way than the latter. The piece illustrated here is an exquisite example of lobed enamel jewellery – the first method of decoration with enamel.  
This is a circular pendant whose form assumes a concave surface. Its decorative layout is arranged along three horizontal sections. The central section, which is the broadest, is filled with an inscription in *kufic* script set in white, decorated in red, and placed against a background of ash-green. The text reads: “… God is best to take care \[of him\]” and is part of verse (*ayah*) 64 of the Chapter of Joseph (*Yusuf*; no. 12). The sections above and below the inscription are decorated with a vegetal branch, each of which is depicted in red, and set against a green background.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.short_description: Women used all kinds and shapes of jewellery, such as bracelets, rings, earrings, brooches and pendants. Techniques in ornamentation included engraving, incising, piercing and enamel inlay. This piece is good example of decorative enamel inlay.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.method_for_datation: The pendant is dated by means of studying the *kufic* script used in the decoration. Dating was also greatly assisted by a comparative study of the pendant's craftsmanship that, together with some objects made of stucco, have been uncovered in archaeological excavations in the Egyptian City of Fustat, and which are attributed to the same period.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.method_for_provenance: A study of the pendant's craftsmanship with reference to stucco objects also uncovered in archaeological excavations in Fustat suggests that the pendant may have been produced there.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.obtention: The object was discovered during the course of archaeological excavations that took place in Fustat in 1916.

baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.name: Breast Ornament
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.description:
Jewellery reached its zenith in the 18th century. Monarchs throughout Europe – from Lisbon to Dresden; England to Naples – wore jewellery to reinforce their majesty and political power. High standards of craftsmanship together with up-to-date designs supplied the luxurious and ostentatious Portuguese court of Kings João V (1706–1750) , José I (1750–1777) and Queen D. Maria I.  
At this time of Portuguese Absolutism, the magnificence of Portuguese jewellery is closely linked with the colonisation of Brazil, with enormous quantities of gold pouring into the kingdom (from 1699) and diamonds (from 1729) onwards. Greater quantities of precious gems were mined in Brazil, in Rio das Velhas, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso and Bahía, further increasing the materials available.  
This particular ornamental breast jewellery – which would have adorned a lady's dress – is a remarkable example from the period. So many bejewelled women would have added to the splendour of court life, its balls and receptions. The naturalism of this piece together with the asymmetrical composition confirms that the fashions emanating from the French court of Louis XV were extremely popular, although from the late 1760s this gave way to the Rococo style exemplified by softer and more graceful shapes of exceptional beauty.  
This piece of jewellery was designed as a single piece with the exception of the garland topping it which was added later. Ornaments such as this one were often constructed in stand-alone parts so they could be worn separately. The silver structure is set with chrysoberyls, garnets, yellow topazes, colourless gem-stones quartz, beryl and topaz. The array of colourful gems includes green and blue doublets and, as usual then, a fair number of quartz and topaz backed with various shades of coloured foil to create striking variations of light and colour.
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.short_description: Costume jewellery of this kind was a magnificent addition to a lady’s dress. Typologically it relates to the fashionable aristocratic jewellery of the European courts from the second half of the 18th century. It is also a direct consequence of the Portuguese colonisation of Brazil.
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.method_for_datation: The piece was brought to the MNSR on 3 August 1945 from the Royal Treasury of Oporto by the goldsmith and researcher José Rosas Júnior.

bb98e522-f646-5d72-a9f4-01e1cce27fbd.name: Brooch (Amulet)
bb98e522-f646-5d72-a9f4-01e1cce27fbd.short_description: Originally a heart-shaped amulet with a longitudinal perforation at the top which allowed it to be strung and hung. It was later set in a gold-and-enamel mount, fitted with a clasp, and served as a brooch. The stone features engraved and gilded Arabic inscriptions in *naskhi* and in *nasta'liq* script; there are also several inscriptions in low relief. The texts along the border reproduce in their entirety four of the last Suras, starting at the top, from right to left, as follows: Sura CIX (*Al Kafirun* / *The Disbelievers*), Sura CXII (*Al Ikhlas* / *Sincerity*), Sura CXIV (*Al Nas* / *Mankind*), and Sura CXIII (*Al Falaq* / *The Daybreak*). Other inscriptions are incorporated into a vegetal design whose large leaves are used as epigraphic cartouches. At the bottom, the invocation ‘*Ya ‘Ali!*’ (‘O ‘Ali!’). The texts are either excerpts from the Qur’an, such as verse 13 from Sura XIII (*Al Ra’d* / *The Thunder*) and verse 13 from Sura LXI (*Al Saff* / *The Ranks*), or formulas exalting the divine power and invocations which include several of the ninety-nine names of Allah. Also inscribed on the stone are the Muslim profession of faith, *shahada* (‘there is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah’), and the invocation ‘*Ya Muhammad!*’ (‘O Muhammad!’).

bc65e295-73e5-5ae4-84e4-1777b2658828.name: Bracelet
bc65e295-73e5-5ae4-84e4-1777b2658828.short_description:
Hollow domes and welded reliefs with locking mechanism. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom.  
The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for these purposes. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

bd425b9a-5df3-53ae-8d59-3df33045cb72.name: Pair of fibulae.
bd425b9a-5df3-53ae-8d59-3df33045cb72.description:
Each of the two fibulae consists of a sliding tongue on an arch and a decorative body finished on the edge opposite the pin with a small ring intended to fix the chain that joined the two fibulae. The body of the fibula is ovoid and its decoration arranged radially. Four bezels in the shape of fleurons known as *gharnati* or roses of Rhodes set with two green fluorite stones and two garnets emanate from an oval medallion studded with a green fluorite stone. Foliate compositions consisting of double grooved palms and three symmetrical palms in the shape of fleurons also emerge from the centre. These are decorated with baroque pearls attached to the surface of the piece with gold wire fixed with a small golden ball. The edges of the fibula are decorated with double palms whose lobes curl in different directions to form a line of festoons.  
This valuable, practical piece of jewellery was intended to hold up the bride's *haik* (robe) and includes a prophylactic symbol against the evil eye. In fact, the cruciform arrangement consisting of five stones suggests the five-fingered hand motif as well as the central eye that sees danger and scatters it to the four winds to protect the new bride or wife who wears it from any misfortune that the envious may wish upon her.
bd425b9a-5df3-53ae-8d59-3df33045cb72.short_description: These fibulae have sliding pin, semi-circular fastenings and were used to fix a bride's dress. These are coupled with a plaque decorated on both sides to complete the piece. One side is enamelled and the other studded with five precious stones, the symbol of the hand.

Cameos like this one continued to be made in later centuries, often by Indian lapidaries, and set into jewelled pendants to be worn.

c644f172-5e30-55ce-9c9e-f557428c4c25.name: Hand of Fatima
c644f172-5e30-55ce-9c9e-f557428c4c25.short_description:
This object represents the "Hand of Fatima" also known as *Khamsa* (the Arabic word for "Five"), "Hand of Venus" or "Aphrodite". Jewish silversmiths in Morocco became known for casting and engraving pieces such as this one, used as a talismanic doorknob or jewellery pendant.  
  
Carthaginian excavations traced the open hand to ancient Egypt, whose variations appear across all faiths and time as a representation of God and believed to grant protection against ill will. In Islam, Fatima, the beloved daughter of Prophet Muhammed (PBUH) defends anyone regardless of faith against evil.  
  
The hand appears symmetrical with the five fingers indistinguishable, embodying the secret codes of the number five in Islam. The fingers allude to the five pillars of Islam, five daily prayers and five keys to the unseen. While silver casts additional amuletic power, the phoenix and salamanders symbolize life, rebirth and fertility.

c8cfe806-d0a6-52f3-8548-dbfaefacc927.name: *Khatim bu Fas* (Finger Ring) with Crescent Moon and Stars
c8cfe806-d0a6-52f3-8548-dbfaefacc927.short_description:
The sun, moon, stars and planets guided early Omani navigators across oceans and deserts, and the observation of celestial phenomena gave rise to the lunar calendar as a schedule around which to plan habitual activities. In Islam, astronomical observation signals the start of the Holy Month of Ramadan and the *Hajj* (pilgrimage season) and determines the timing of daily prayers.  
  
Omani artisans use celestial symbols as expressions of the Islamic faith and universal representations of the natural world. Crescent moons and stars are especially prevalent in jewellery, ceremonial weaponry and in all forms of architectural adornment. Sun and earth emblems and constellations are also occasionally seen.

ca59fd60-c057-5dbf-a2fa-484dcab24b97.name: Ring
ca59fd60-c057-5dbf-a2fa-484dcab24b97.short_description: Thin silver ring with oval-shaped agate stone set in silver with inherent decoration on the soundings. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for this purpose. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.name: One of a pair of earrings.
cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.description:
Gold manufacturing has been known in Syria from at least 2000 BC. Gold artefacts, moulds, and various goldsmiths' tools have been found in numerous Syrian archaeological sites, including those at Ugarit, Mushrifa, and Ebla. During the Classical period, gold jewellery was widely produced in Syria, particularly in Hawran, Palmyra (Tadmur) and Homs.  
The development of gold manufacturing in Syria continued during the Islamic period, as exemplified by surviving examples such as this single earring, made from woven gold in the form of a circular disk with radiating edges lined by a string of pearls. In the centre of the disc is a triangular formation of two red rubies and a green emerald. A circular ruby instead of a pearl indicates the top side of the disc, out of which protrudes a link to another triangular set of three precious stones mirroring the ones on the filigree disk, a green emerald and two red rubies set within gold mounts. Above them, located near the ear wire, is a final decorative feature of a little pierced golden sphere also containing a precious stone; an emerald.
cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.short_description: This gold filigree earring encrusted with precious emeralds, rubies and pearls indicates the high quality of jewellery production for which the Fatimid period is famed. Similar finds from Egypt and Syria abound.
cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.method_for_datation: The production of highly refined gold jewellery flourished in Egypt and Syria during the Fatimid period (358–567 / AD 969–1171). The techniques employed included filigree and a method using granules of gold; twisted rope-like gold, and occasionally inlay work with gems were also employed. Products include bracelets, armlets, earrings, pendants, rings, belts, brooches, and hair ornaments.
cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.method_for_provenance: During the Fatimid period, the gold-production centres of Syria and Egypt flourished, particularly those in Aleppo and Cairo. Although this item was obtained by the Museum from Raqqa, it is not possible to determine the provenance of this object definitively.

d3f8650a-4599-5d0e-a22f-cd44a5f3ea38.name: The Pietroasa Treasure
d3f8650a-4599-5d0e-a22f-cd44a5f3ea38.short_description: One of the most valuable gold treasures of Romania is the Pietroasa hoard, which consists of five golden vessels and seven golden pieces of jewelry with a total weight of 19 kg. Dating from the centuries 4-5 AD, the hoard is attributed to the Goths. It was discovered accidentally in April 1837 by two peasants who sold it to an Albanian contractor named Verussi. Knowing that all treasures found in the Romanian soil had to be handed in to the authorities, Verussi tried to hide the hoard and even smashed some of the items to make them smaller. Even though he was eventually caught by the police, from the initial 22 items of the hoard only 12 were recuperated. The Pietroasa treasure was first internationally exhibited in 1867 at the universal exposition in Paris, where it enjoyed a great success.

d4f761e5-39cf-5040-a028-277cc5dd0f2b.short_description: This pendant was used on the horses of Ottoman officials and indicated their high status and wealth. It is made of a single, lozenge-shaped silver plaque decorated with turquoise, burgundy and blue gemstones. Short, thin silver chains with leaf-shaped pendants dangle from this plaque and produce a tinkling noise when moving, announcing the arrival of the rider.

d7bfd409-e2ad-54bc-aea9-cbf7cee1a22d.name: Bridal jewellery worn on the breasts (*Mingjuska so vot* and necklace)
d7bfd409-e2ad-54bc-aea9-cbf7cee1a22d.short_description: This piece of jewellery provides evidence on the versatility of articles of adornment worn by women in Macedonia in the 19th century. *Mingjushka so vot* belongs to the group of jewellery decorating the chests, although there is no clear distinction from pieces worn around the neck. This exquisite breast jewellery consists of a rectangular piece of broadcloth – *klashna* – covered with small silver coins reminiscent of fish scales and adorned with decorative stones. It is bordered by a chain, which is additionally adorned with coins. It used to be worn suspended on a chain. Abundant ornamentation with coins was applied on diverse pieces of jewellery and articles of adornment within all ethnic communities in Macedonia.

dbac428e-60fa-534a-a05b-62093f37af08.name: Necklace.
dbac428e-60fa-534a-a05b-62093f37af08.description: Gold necklace (*al-haiathe*) consisting of four tubular beads alternating with oblong beads. There are two opposed pyramid-shaped pieces, one at either end, that link together. The necklace has three pendants. The middle one is made up of two oblong beads, similar to the ones on the necklace, and a piece known as an *alcorci*, the centre of which would once have been decorated with a glaze, and a pyramid-shaped piece that would have linked to another, now lost. The *alcorci* is made up of two thin sheets with a hollow space between them, which is characteristic of the Nasrid items in the treasure troves at Mondujar, from which this piece came, and Bentarique (Almería). This lotus flower structure was thought to derive from the Hand of Fatima, but a more recent hypothesis suggests a more probable origin in Central Asia, with parallels in Ottoman fabrics. More direct references can be seen in the panels of Córdoban Caliphate palace of Madinat al-Zahra. The lateral pendants are made up of an oblong bead, a small spherical bead and a pyramid-shaped end piece. The techniques used are perforated metal in the tubular beads and filigree in the pendants. This is a piece of exceptionally fine finish and delicacy. The necklace has been strung at random; the different parts being used separately to embellish clothes, headdresses or hair, as recorded in literary sources ('and the women put gold in the hair on their heads', reads one manuscript).
dbac428e-60fa-534a-a05b-62093f37af08.short_description: Some of the few items of Nasrid jewellery to have survived have been found in hidden collections of valuable items, such as the Mondujar Treasure in Granada from which this necklace stands out, with its fine fretwork and twisted-wire filigree, undoubtedly the work of a skilled goldsmith.
dbac428e-60fa-534a-a05b-62093f37af08.dimensions: Length 47 cm, width 2.8 cm, length of pendant 11 cm.
dbac428e-60fa-534a-a05b-62093f37af08.method_for_datation: The stylistic features (the very delicate gold sheets, the filigree technique) and parallels with contemporary pieces enable us to attribute this piece to the Kingdom of Granada. It is also part of the well-dated Nasrid treasure trove at Mondujar (Granada).
dbac428e-60fa-534a-a05b-62093f37af08.method_for_provenance: This piece, along with Nasrid treasure trove it came from, was discovered at Mondujar in the province of Granada.
dbac428e-60fa-534a-a05b-62093f37af08.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum from Juan Ignacio Miró on 8 November 1869.

deefaabe-b27a-5afa-b282-2ebbb01847c5.name: Single earring.
deefaabe-b27a-5afa-b282-2ebbb01847c5.description:
The filigree earring is composed of a circular tube of gold foil, soldered onto the inside of which is a piece that consists of freestanding decorative elements, which decorate only the earring’s lower half. On one side there is an eyelet clasp. Freestanding wire-work and surface granulation create what looks like a rosette, which is framed on either side by two rectangular boxes. The rosette is composed of six simple circles bordered by a crenellated frieze made of granulated dots. Six circles fill the rectangular boxes. Two friezes of differing width sit above the rosette and boxes, each consisting of a horizontal row of circles. Further individual elements are soldered onto the gold tube as well as to each other, achieving a certain stability or solidity while retaining an apparent lightness of structure.  
The designers and makers of women’s jewellery in the Umayyad and Abbasid periods took their inspiration from examples that were made in the Byzantine era, so that designs changed only gradually. The earring’s geometry expresses the decorative aesthetic of the time, an aesthetic evident within other art forms such as architectural decoration.
deefaabe-b27a-5afa-b282-2ebbb01847c5.short_description: This single earring from early Islamic Egypt follows a shape in use in pre-Islamic times. The design within the lower part of the circle has an almost architectural quality. A medallion and friezes contain differently executed rows of small circles. This type of jewellery was made for woman.
deefaabe-b27a-5afa-b282-2ebbb01847c5.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
deefaabe-b27a-5afa-b282-2ebbb01847c5.method_for_datation: This type of earring and the design of each individual element point to it being from Late Antiquity or the Byzantine era, so that the earliest date that can be suggested is some time within the Early Islamic period.
deefaabe-b27a-5afa-b282-2ebbb01847c5.method_for_provenance: The earring was acquired in Cairo and strikingly similar examples can be seen in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo, so it is very likely that it is of Egyptian provenance.

e204df2a-1723-53bc-98dd-25fd21837af9.name: Bracelet
e204df2a-1723-53bc-98dd-25fd21837af9.description: Antoinette Riklin-Schelbert belonged to the avant-garde of Swiss jewellery makers. Trained as a silversmith, she ran her own studio and shop after 1946. She exhibited at national and international shows, published books, and gave lectures. She also held the post of president of the Swiss Crafts Council from 1986 to 1992. The SNM’s two collections – comprising Riklin-Schelbert’s own designs and those of other contemporary Swiss makers as well as her sketchbooks – reflect her role as a pioneer of experimental jewellery and her influence on other jewellery makers in Switzerland.

e4a3c365-57ac-5446-beee-1e9f89dbe76e.name: Fragment of a brooch.
e4a3c365-57ac-5446-beee-1e9f89dbe76e.description:
Fragment of a brooch consisting of a body and a clasp. The body of the brooch is composed of a plaque curved into the shape of a small jug. On each side, two small rings have been soldered on, taking on the appearance of two small handles. Two more rings have been soldered to the top of the body, and onto these the remains of a clasp is fixed. The clasp is composed of one of the rings, soldered onto a tongue (of a buckle) that is pushed through the two rings and ends in a small ball, which is used to keep the clasp shut.  
The central part is better decorated, with incised dots executed across the entire surface in sets of three. At the centre, two types of spread out leaves have been traced out, one within the other. The inner leaf is embellished with small silver granules. The space between these two leaves remains devoid all of decoration. Two twisted wires of silver have been soldered onto the lower part of the brooch.  
This fragment of a brooch was an object of finery that was worn on top of clothes. The buckle that was used to fix the brooch to cloth is missing.
e4a3c365-57ac-5446-beee-1e9f89dbe76e.short_description: Brooch fragment consisting of a jug-shaped curved plate decorated with dots carved in threes and a motif consisting of two leaves, one inside the other. The small rings on either side look like handles, and the rings on one end were used to fix what remains of the clasp.
e4a3c365-57ac-5446-beee-1e9f89dbe76e.dimensions: Length 3.39 cm, width 1.1 cm, weight 3 g.
e4a3c365-57ac-5446-beee-1e9f89dbe76e.method_for_datation: Bourouiba dates this fragment of brooch to the Hammadid era without offering justification. This hypothesis is challenged by an inscription featured on a medallion found alongside this fragment that was written in *naskhi* characters (cursive), a script particular to the Almohads and the Hafsids, and not the Hammadids, who used *kufic* lettering. Furthermore, this brooch fragment was brought to light along with thousands of Almohad coins and one Hafsid coin. It would thus make sense to date it to the 7th / 13th century.
e4a3c365-57ac-5446-beee-1e9f89dbe76e.method_for_provenance: Bourouiba states, in the *Bulletin d'archéologie algérienne* (Vol. III, 1968), that the fragment was discovered 'in the western part of the prayer hall of the mosque of the Qal'a of the Bani Hammad, near the last pillar of the penultimate nave, to the right of the *mihrab*'.

e55614b8-f79a-5fa9-af73-256d887343b2.name: Pectoral plate
e55614b8-f79a-5fa9-af73-256d887343b2.short_description: Besides the obvious decorative purposes, jewellery in such heavily tribal societies indicates ethnic identity and social status. Turkoman jewellery is usually gilded; both gold and brass were used. Carnelian is the stone of choice used for inlay. It is believed to protect the wearer from death and sickness besides bringing happiness and peace. Amuletic jewellery, called *tumar*, is worn among all Turkoman tribes. *Tumar*s are classified as pectorals as they are worn around the neck and fall over the chest, although they can reach as far as the waist. This large silver pectoral features a double-headed bird, which since ancient times has been a symbol of power and authority.
e55614b8-f79a-5fa9-af73-256d887343b2.bibliography: Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia, *Jewellery of the Islamic World: An Introduction*, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2009: 32-33, 62-66.

e7628812-bff0-56db-90f6-eba9949466d5.name: Pair of Bracelets with Chased Decoration
e7628812-bff0-56db-90f6-eba9949466d5.short_description: *Hujuls* (Bracelets) such as these from the al-Busaid Dynasty, sometimes worn as anklets, were worn in paired sets by women and children in Central and Northern Oman. Small stones sealed inside rattle with the movement of wearer. These are fine examples of one of Oman's oldest design elements, circles with central dots. Its use on shell jewellery has been dated to the 4th millennium BC. More complex dot-in-circle patterns are found on 3rd and 2nd millennium BC soft-stone vessels where they are typically arranged in rows and combined with linear elements. Today dot-in-circle patterns continue to be used by Omani artisans working in clay, wood, copper, silver and many other materials. They are seen on wooden drums, axe blades and knife scabbards of the Musandam Peninsula, on the silver jewellery of northern Oman and on the pottery of Dhofar.
e7628812-bff0-56db-90f6-eba9949466d5.obtention: Museum of the Ministry of Heritage and Culture
keywords: Hujul; Bracelet; Silver; Jewellery; Dot-in-Circle

ea93f27b-2ec2-5723-a1f1-65b29d221852.name: *Talahiq* (Gunpowder Horn)
ea93f27b-2ec2-5723-a1f1-65b29d221852.short_description:
Arabic is a poetic language with expressive power, and Omanis are known to be articulate and moving storytellers and poets. Arabic calligraphy, prized as a means of communication and adornment, gives form to literary expression within a visual context. The traditional art of verbal expression remains popular in Oman today, and master poets and storytellers are held in high esteem. Proverbs, whether recited or written, serve as a means of imparting wisdom and human truths based on common sense and often take the form of a metaphor or a poem. Sources of proverbs include the sayings of the Prophet Muhammed and other thinkers and theologians.  
  
This gunpowder horn, which comes from the period of Imam Said bin Ahmed al-Busai’idi (r. 1783-1810 AD), the 2nd ruler of the al-Busai’idi of Oman and the son of Imam Ahmed, founder of the al-Busai’idi Dynasty, was designed to fill the powder pan of a matchlock gun. The large decorative top was removable for filling the horn, and the gunpowder was released at the narrow end by operating the lever along the inner curve. The horn is made of silver, which has been layered with gold, and it is decorated with stamped and chased work suggesting that it belonged to a prominent person. An extract of a poem by al-Mutannabi, a renowned 10th century AD poet, is inscribed on the side of the horn:  
  
'If death is inevitable ... Then it is shameful to die a coward.'

ebbbddf3-9839-58cb-8991-7b2a32983ed3.name: Casting mould.
ebbbddf3-9839-58cb-8991-7b2a32983ed3.description:
Rectangular, slightly trapezoidal, slate engraved on both sides. In each of its four corners there are holes and pivots used to attach the other half of the casting mould. On one of the faces, between two parallel lines that delineate the central area, there is a six-petal flower within a sunken circle, and below that a sprue for the molten metal. The other face, with its corresponding pivots, holes and sprue, includes a small disk that resembles a coin bearing a three-line *kufic* inscription and a ring for hanging it up on top.  
This type of mould with two separate shells that could be used on both sides enabled the serial production of small items of jewellery such as pendants and amulets. The metal would have been melted in a crucible and poured into the mould to obtain the desired shape and, once it had cooled and solidified, it would only have required minor touching up with the appropriate tools.  
Although middle-class Andalusian women would have regularly worn this type of adornment, very few remains of this type of jewellery have survived, probably because the metal was continuously refounded and reused.
ebbbddf3-9839-58cb-8991-7b2a32983ed3.short_description: This mould was used for mass-producing low-cost jewellery for people of modest status. The shape of the piece was carved out of each of the two halves, which were then joined together so that liquid metal could be poured in through the funnels. The resulting piece was polished by hand.
ebbbddf3-9839-58cb-8991-7b2a32983ed3.dimensions: Height 5 cm, width 3.4 cm, depth 0.7 cm.
ebbbddf3-9839-58cb-8991-7b2a32983ed3.method_for_datation: This slate is part of a group of four casting mould shells that probably came from the same small jeweller's workshop. The decorative and epigraphic motifs engraved in them allow us to date them to the Caliphate period.
ebbbddf3-9839-58cb-8991-7b2a32983ed3.method_for_provenance: According to the paperwork, these pieces were bought from the great researcher, archaeologist and historian Manuel Gómez Moreno (Granada 1870–Madrid 1970), who suggested a potential origin of San Esteban de Gormaz, Soria.

ebbbddf3-9839-58cb-8991-7b2a32983ed3.obtention: The piece is one of a number of moulds acquired by the State through Ministerial Order of 30 April 1958. The exact date it came to the National Archaeological Museum is unknown.

eeb73625-9b7f-5b6e-bac6-70835ba47781.name: Amulet
eeb73625-9b7f-5b6e-bac6-70835ba47781.short_description: Tear-shaped pendant with a silver openwork border of twisted wire and granulation. It is inscribed on both sides with Arabic repoussé invocations and Qur’anic texts. The invocations in *thuluth* script on the scrolling ground at the centre are surrounded by epigraphic bands with verses in *naskhi* calligraphy: ‘*Ma sha’ Allah!*’ (‘God willing’) is encircled by the verses of Sura CXIII (*Al-Falaq*/ *The Daybreak*) and ‘*Ya Hafiz!*’ (‘O Preserver!’), by the verses of Sura CXIV (*Al-Nas* / *Mankind*). These last two chapters of the Qur’an, very short and intensely evocative, referred to as *al-mu‘awwidhatan* (the two protecting ones), appear quite frequently on amulets.

f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.name: Headdress
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.short_description: Three bands of silver chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head and attached to a surrounding fabric patterned in minute beadwork and sewn with various Ottoman and Russian coins. From this head-piece hangs a long piece of cotton sewn with coins of the Ottoman Empire with a rectangular pendant and multiple red and green silk tassels on the back. Headdresses like this one were worn by married women, as silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride. The Ottoman and Russian coins reflect the social and economic situation of Jordan between the end of the 19th century and the early 20th century, when it was part of the Ottoman empire and it was influenced by population movements, demographic changes and trade with distant countries.

f5eca8aa-876e-503f-b619-df15835f81aa.name: Necklace
f5eca8aa-876e-503f-b619-df15835f81aa.short_description: This silver necklace from Grande Kabylie was traditionally worn on a woman's bosom to hold the *ddill*, a finely woven cloth worn by women of the region. It is made of of two ornate brooches with a coral in the centre, connected by a gold chain necklace to which the jeweller has added various French coins (francs) that were no longer in use. A number of jewellers used coins to decorate their jewellery. They usually used coins which had suddenly gone out of use.

f9783bd6-7a5b-5ca2-8a70-781a2af32872.name: Cross chain
f9783bd6-7a5b-5ca2-8a70-781a2af32872.short_description: A cross of silver on a silver chain known with the folkloric name “heal of gazelle”, worn by Christian women. fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.name: ‘Eye of envy’ amulet.
fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.description:
A blue 'eye of envy' made of a moulded, blue glass disc decorated with a series of diminishing circles of yellow, then white, with a black spot at the centre. Probably a bead from a string of other similar beads, it has a hole though the side for threading. This type of glass 'eye' might also have been sewn on to garments and headdresses.  
  
Within Islamic popular belief blue eyes are thought to be envious eyes; the eye of envy is worn to repel such negative power by reflecting back to the perpetrator their own envy, thereby protecting the wearer from the effects of jealousy, thought to cause illness or disaster.  
  
Such eyes can be crudely made like this bead, or can be drawn with accuracy and quality of craftsmanship, as found in jewellery made of gold or silver; the quality does not affect the protective power. Plain blue beads are also thought to play a similar protective role, and are sometimes used in place of an eye of envy.
fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.short_description: In popular Middle Eastern Islamic belief blue eyes are thought to be both envious and to have the ability to repel envy. This blue glass eye is worn to protect the bearer from the effects of jealousy, which may cause the loss of what is being envied or illness or disaster.
